caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 103 of 1962.
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Advocate ----- For the Appellant
Md. Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, AAG ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Khorshed Ahmed Chowdhury ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Government of Bangladesh & others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The suit is for declaration that the khas lands of the plaintiff-Wakf Estate measuring 422.41 acres of khas lands as detailed in schedules A-H have not been legally acquired as excess land as the 70 members of the five families of the name of the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury, were entitled to retain 700 bighas of khas land under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the order of the Revenue Officer dated 22.2.56 and Circle Officer dated 23.2.56, allowing only 348.80 acres as Khas land of the plaintiff-wake estate, in illegal, null and void. 

 3. The plaintiffs case is the late Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury was a very rich man and he executed and registered the wakfnama dated 14th Ashar, 1337 BS vide Ext.1 with respect to the suit lands. There were tenants with respect to some part of the suit land and the income from the tenanted land would exceed Tk. 10,000.00. Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury had 422.41 acres of khas land in his possession. The wakfnama was duly enrolled with the Wakf Commissioner and its number is 1261. As per the provisions of the Wakf Deed, the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury was the sole Motwalli till his death. Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury died on 18th Poush, 1341 BS leaving 4 sons namely Fazle Ali Chowdhury, Khorshed Ahmed Chowdhury, Nazir Ahmed Chowdhury and Najibul Hoque Chowdhury. As per the terms of the wakfnama the above 4 sons of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury were to act as Mutwalli for 2 years only by rotation and in case of death of any son, the son of the deceased would act as Mutwalli. The total income from the wakf estate of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury from both the tenanted and Khas land was Tk. 30,000.00 per annum. In the Wakfnama, it is stipulated that each son of the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury would get 60 mds, of paddy and cash of Tk. 2,000.00 annually, The heirs of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury have got 70 members in 5 families. The Wakf was created for religious, "charitable and pious purposes in conformity with the Wakf Validating Act XI of 1910. It is alleged that no special notification under section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was served for acquiring the Khas land of the Wakf Estate and the above orders are illegal, ultra vires, etc, and the officers of the government have been acting without jurisdiction in acquiring the lands. It is alleged that the number of the members in the 5 families of late Abdul Jabbar is 70, they are entitled to retain bighas of Khas lands in their possession and the Revenue Officer and the Circle Officer have acted illegally and without jurisdiction in acquiring the plaintiff's land in the manner done by the impugned orders dated 22.2.56 and 23.2.56 respectively. The plaintiff was, therefore, obliged to file the present suit for declaration. 

 4. Defendant No. 1, the then Province of East Pakistan, contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, on the grounds that the disputed Wakf is an Wakf-ul Awlad and as such the khas lads of the Wakf Estate has been quite legally and rightly acquired by the impugned orders. The allegations and statements made in the plaint arc not true and the same are denied by the defendant. It is contended in the written statement that the plaintiff and other heirs of late Abdul Jabbar the Wakif have got no right, title and interest in the suit lands which are Wakf properties and they are only the beneficiaries of the wakf. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has taken us through the impugned judgment, the evidence and other materials on record. He frankly submitted that the present case will be guided by the principle laid down by the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Shamsuzzoha Nurul Amin Chowdhury and others, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 195, as the facts of the present case are more or less similar to the facts of the above reported case. We have gone through the above case reported in 28 DLR (AD) 195. In that case, their Lordships of the Appellate Division have given interpretation of the law laid down in section 20(5)(i)(c) and (ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows: (5) (i) Nothing in sub-sections (1) and (2) and (3) of this section shall apply-(c) to so much of the lands held under debutter, wakf, wakf-al-al-aulad or any other trust as is exclusively dedicated and the income from which is exclusively applied to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual. (ii) "Where, under any debutter, wakf, wakf-al-al-aulad or any other trust, the income from the lands covered by such trust is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes and partly reserved for the pecuniary benefit of any individual, only such portion of the lands, as may be selected in accordance with the rules to be made in this behalf by the Government, shall come within the purview of sub-clause (c) of clause(i)". 

 8. It is not disputed that the wakfnana Ext. 1 is a Wakf-al-al-aulad as contemplated under section 20(5)(ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such, the wakf property in suit, are liable to be acquired under the above section of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. By the impugned order dated 22.2.56 reproduced in at pages 24-26 Part II of the paper-book, the Revenue Officer allowed 45.36 acres of land to be retained as khas land to meet the expenditure of the charitable deeds mentioned in the wakf deed and 36.39 acres to be retained as Khas land as wakf-al-al-aulad under section 20(5)(ii) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by making the following observation: 

 9. In interpreting the section 20(5)(ii) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, their Lordships of the Appellate Division in para 14 of the above referred case, observed as follows: 

 "In our opinion any wakf-al-al-aulad which is dedicated partly for charitable purpose and partly for individual benefit or wholly for benefit of any individual, the Khas land of such wakf-al-al-aulad estate should be retained on the footing of the living heirs representing the wakf estate on the date the section came into operation. The heirs of the wakif in the aggregate will represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity but not in their personal capacity. Calculated on this basis, the wakf-al-al-aulad estate will retain as much as it will be possible to retain above 100 bighas by as many number as the heirs will be in existence above ten." 

 "According to our judgment, the heirs of the wakf will represent the wakf estate and land will be allotted to the wakf estate on that basis. The land so allotted will be khas land of the wakf estate. If some land in excess is left over on calculation, it will vest in the Government, but the compensation money for the excess land will be wakf and the mutawalli will be bound to re-invest the same in any other suitable property." 

 13. It is not possible for us to decide here as to the actual number of members in the families of the heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury, specially when the learned Subordinate Judge did not at all discuss the point. We therefore, find no other alternative than to send the suit on remand to the Trial Court for framing an issue as to the number of the members of the families of Late Abdul Jabbar and to allow them to retain Khas lands at the rate of 10 standard bighas per member of the families of the heirs of late Abdul Jabbar, as laid down by their Lordships in the above case and also in section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act., discussed above. 

 2. "It is contended by the learned lawyer for the defendant that no proper and valid notice under section 80 of the CPC has been served upon the defendant No. 1 in this suit. Section 80 of the CPC provides that notice under the signature of the person issuing the notice and containing the names of the parties and the cause of action should be served on the Collector when Province is the defendant. In the present suit no copy of such notice has been produced. So assuming that notice under section 80 CPC was actually sent to the Collector, it cannot be said that it was valid and proper notice under section 80 CPC. Moreover PW 4 Azizul Gaffar Chowdhury, the original plaintiff says in his deposition that he sent the notice under section 80 CPC to the Collector by his signature and he (PW4) cannot say what was the contents of the said notice. Plaintiff has filed postal receipt Ext. 3 and the postal acknowledgement receipt No. 4 in order to prove that the notice under section 80 CPC has been duly served upon the Collector. But with reference to Ext. 4 it appears that one Kiron Chandra Guha, pleader, Amanat Ganj Barisal has signed the alleged notice, PW 2 pro-defendant No. 3 also cannot say what has been written in the notice under section 80 CPC. Notice under section 80 is mandatory. So it is incumbent on the plaintiff to prove that proper, sufficient and valid notice under section 80 CPC was served upon the proper authority. But on the material on record as stated above I am unable to hold that valid and proper notice was served upon the defendant No. 1. Hence I hold that there has not been any valid and proper notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure in this suit." 

 15. In para 26 of the plaint, it is stated that notice under section 80 CPC was served upon the Collector, Bakerganj representing the Province of East Pakistan on 5.2.60 and the postal and acknowledgment receipt are admittedly filed in Court which are marked as Exts. 3 and 4 respectively. From Exts. 3 and 4, it is clear that the notice was sent to the Collector, Bakerganj and it was received by his office, In para 20 of the written statement, it is stated that there was no valid or proper notice under section 80 CPC. The defendant did not deny the service of notice. Their contention was that the notice was not valid or proper. The defendant did not say in which respect, the notice is not valid or not proper. Section 80 CPC does not contemplate the validity or invalidity of notice among proper notice. Absence of service of notice cannot be a ground for dismissal of the suit, as it is evident from 80 CPC itself. Section 80 CPC runs as follows: 

 (ii) in the case of a suit against the Government relating to the affairs of the Railway, the General Manager of the Railway and in the case of a public officer, delivered to him or left at his office stating the cause of action, the name, description of place of residence of the plaintiff and the relief which he claims; and the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left. 

 (2) Where any such suit is instituted without delivering or leaving such notice as aforesaid or before the expiration of the said period of two months or where the plaint does not contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left, the plaintiff shall not be entitled to any costs if settlement as regards the subject-matter of the suit is reached or the Government or the public officer concedes the plaintiffs claim, within the period of two months from the date of the institution of the suit: 

 Provided that in a suit instituted without such notice, the Court shall allow not less than three months to the Government to submit its written statement." 

 18. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant contends that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that Article 14 is applicable in the present case. He submits that in the present case, Article 120 is applicable. In support of this contention, he put reliance on a decision reported in 21 DLR 492. As already stated, that the present suit is a suit for declaration and not for setting aside the impugned order and, as such, the suit is governed by Article 120 which provides limitation for 6 years. The impugned order was passed on 22.2.56 and 23.2.56 and the suit was filed on 12.8.60 i.e. within 6 years from the date of the impugned orders. The suit was thus filed within time. We, therefore, decide the issue No. 3 in favour of the plaintiff-appellant by setting aside the finding of the Trial Court on this issue. 

 "2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, application and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Ord. No. III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made by any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect; and no court shall entertain, and no person shall bring, any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question." 

 20. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that the above provision of PO 90/72 is violative of the fundamental right of the plaintiff as laid down in the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, it is void. He further contends that even assuming that the above PO is a good piece of law, in that case also the present suit does not come within the mischief of the above provision of the PO 90/72 which prohibits suits challenging the legality and validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or "of the acquisition of any property made by any provision thereof", as the suit property has not yet been acquired by the Government and it was in the process of acquisition when the suit was filed, He submits that the parties were asked to maintain status-quo with respect to the acquisition of the suit properties by order dated 24.6.60 by the Trial Court. From the perusal of the record of the Trial Court, it appears that the contention of the learned Advocate is correct. It seems that the plaintiff-appellant is still in possession of the suit properties or at any rate this suit property was not finally acquired by service of notice as required under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It may be pointed out that the process of acquisition became final only after publication of the notification in the official Gazette under sub-section 2 of section 43 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, declaring that the compensation assessment roll has been finally published. The property vests in the Government only after the above notification as laid down in section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in published. Without entering into the investigation as to whether PO 90/72 is violative of the provisions of the Constitution, we are of opinion that the present case does not come within the mischief of section 2 of PO 90/72 and the appeal or the suit is not liable to abate. In view of the above facts and circumstances and the legal position discussed the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set aside.
